claims.text: A controlled low-level chromium addition during vacuum arc melting will form Cr-rich grain-boundary phases or protective chromium-oxide layers in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The resulting Cr-rich phases or oxide layers will enhance high-temperature creep resistance.
The chromium-derived microstructure will enhance high-temperature tensile strength.
The chromium addition will not increase alloy density.
The chromium addition will not compromise room-temperature mechanical performance.
Chromium added in controlled amounts segregates to grain boundaries.
Segregated chromium forms stable grain-boundary phases or oxides.
Cr-rich phases or oxides enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
Cr-rich phases or oxides improve resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
Fine Cr-rich precipitates or a protective Cr-oxide grain-boundary layer improve high-temperature microstructural stability and reduce creep.
Relative to the chromium-free baseline, the chromium-added alloy will show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature creep resistance at 800–1000°C.
Relative to the chromium-free baseline, the chromium-added alloy will show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature tensile strength at 800–1000°C.
The chromium-added alloy will maintain room-temperature strength comparable to that of the chromium-free baseline.
The chromium-added alloy will maintain density comparable to that of the chromium-free baseline.
The beneficial effect is restricted to an optimized low-chromium concentration range.
Chromium contents above the optimized range could produce unwanted phases or increase density.
Testing at 800–1000°C represents high-temperature conditions relevant to jet-turbine operation.
